![The Cheapest Ladder Is Also the Shortest](./cover.png)

This essay is about why maths has always been the cheapest subject to be good
at, and why the thing it now leads to costs a great deal more than a pencil.

Every school subject sends your parents a bill. Most of them just don't break it
down for you. Chemistry wants a lab. Music wants an instrument, and somebody free
on Saturday mornings to drive you to the lesson. Essays want a childhood of being
read to — ten years of free tutoring, dressed up as bedtime.

Maths wants a pencil.

That's the whole bill. You can do serious mathematics on the back of a receipt,
and nobody can tell from the working whether you did it at a desk or on a bus.
Which is why maths is quietly full of broke kids.

## Nobody can argue you out of a proof

The cheapness gets all the attention. I think the bigger draw is something else.
Maths tells you when you're right. It doesn't need an adult's permission to do
it.

Picture being twelve in a house where the rules move without notice. The same
thing gets a laugh on Monday and a row on Tuesday. The grown-ups tell the story
of last week wrong, and you were standing right there when it happened. Now hand
that kid a proof.

The proof doesn't have moods. It isn't different today. Nobody can look them in
the eye and tell them it says something else. They can check it themselves, at
eleven at night, with no help from anyone, and simply *know*. Then they can keep
that somewhere nobody can get at it.

I don't think that's a small thing. I think it might be the whole thing. Maths
isn't only the subject a poor kid can afford. It's the subject that holds still,
and if not much else in your life holds still, that pull is enormous.

## The pattern turns up everywhere I've been

So the sharp, broke kids go into maths. I grew up poor in London, and I've since
spent time in Mexico City, Guadalajara, Guatemala City, Bogotá and Manila. Same
story in all six. Different languages, same kid at the back, three chapters
ahead of everyone, because the problems are the one thing that's always there.

That's six cities and a lifetime of stories, not data. I have no numbers, and
I'd be suspicious of anyone who said they did.

Here's what nobody mentioned to any of us: the ladder is shorter than it looks.

## The bill arrives at twenty-two

Entry costs a pencil. Exit costs about a decade.

You get recruited on the first price. That one is honest, advertised, and close
to zero. The second price never comes up: years of low pay after school, and the
people you'd need to know to turn all those qualifications into actual money.
Partly that's because the people best placed to quote it are the ones who never
had to pay it.

And where you end up is fine! Teaching, statistics, working out insurance risk
for a living: real jobs, stable, respectable, the kind that make your family
proud of you at weddings. They also sit well below where the same brain lands
with a family behind it. Nobody lied. The subject kept every promise it made. It
just made fewer promises than you thought it had.

## There's a way off the ladder, and it's a browser tab

Now the good news, and I do think this is good news.

Every web browser on earth has a place inside it where you can type code and run
it on the spot. It's called the JavaScript console. Right-click on any page, hit
Inspect, and you're in. No licence, no install, no permission, no adult, no
money. A sharp fifteen-year-old who ended up doing maths because maths was the
affordable option can be running real code within the minute. And writing code
pays what proving theorems does not.

It's the same trick maths pulled. Cheap. You can check it yourself, without
asking anybody. You type the thing, it works or it doesn't, and the machine has
no opinion about who your parents are.

I find that genuinely cheering. Then I think about what it actually needs, and
I stop finding it cheering.

## But it charges rent on the room

Not the machine. Or not only the machine, which is the part everyone talks about.

It needs a desk, or something you can pretend is a desk. A chair. A socket that
works, and power that stays on. A couple of hours where nobody else wants the
table for dinner, ironing, homework or a card game. And quiet — not silence,
just enough calm to hold a half-finished idea in your head while somebody walks
through the room. When you're learning to build things, a half-finished idea is
the only kind you ever have.

A phone won't cover it. I know everyone has a phone. But you cannot sit at a
phone for three hours. Everything that makes it good on the bus makes it
hopeless for building.

A pencil asks for none of this, and that is the entire point of a pencil. It
works on the floor. It works on the bus. It works in ten-minute scraps of time
stolen between whatever else people want from you. Of everything in this essay,
it's the only tool that doesn't care what room it's in.

Which is the part that gets me. The kid this whole essay is about is the one who
fell for maths because home didn't hold still. That is exactly the kid with no
quiet corner and no free evening. The thing that pulled them into maths is the
same thing that keeps them there.

So the new ladder pays better than the old one, and it's harder to get onto.
Worse, the moment that decides who gets on has moved somewhere nobody is
watching. It isn't admissions. It isn't the scholarship, or the exam. It happens
years before any of those, in whether the house had a corner that was yours for
two hours and a socket that worked. I don't know how you'd pay for that. I'm not
sure many of the people handing out money know it's the thing to pay for.

Maths was cheap because it never asked about the room you were standing in. The
new one asks for the room.

Maths. Cost. A. Pencil. Computing. Costs. A. Room. Fund. Rooms.
